Open Indus, an open research group

Decipher the Indus script by 2027

Nothing is deciphered yet, and we test every route to a reading in public.

Help decipher it Read the findings

01The script

The writing of a vast early civilisation is still unread

About four thousand short texts survive from the Indus cities, 2600 to 1900 BCE, most on stone seals.

The cities rivalled those of Egypt and Mesopotamia in size and planning, yet left nothing we can read.

So we do not know their language, what they called their cities, or who ruled them. The script is the only direct evidence.

02Where we are

We know how the signs are arranged, but not what they say

Track the progress

03Found so far

The signs follow rules, but no one can read them yet

  • The signs come in a set order, like words in a sentence. Shown texts it has never seen, our model spots the real order 40% of the time. Guessing gets 6%.
  • Some seals break that order. Round seals, mostly found around the Persian Gulf, arrange the signs differently. They may write a foreign language, follow their own style, or not be writing at all.
  • No claimed decipherment holds up. We tested five published claims to have cracked the script. None did better than random guessing.

All eleven findings, with their evidence

04How we work

Every claim is attacked before we publish it

Before running a test, we write down what would count as success, so we cannot move the goalposts afterwards. Any result that looks like progress then goes to a second team whose only job is to break it. We even test whether the signs are writing at all.

Our approach and what counts as done

05Help

The fastest help is an AI agent working an open task

Point a Claude Fable or Opus class agent at an open task, or bring data, photographs or a careful eye. To follow along, get results by email.
